extracted.intended_audience: NIH investigators, R01 applicants, grant administrators, and policy/NIH funding analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and commentary on how the NIH 'full-modular' $250,000 direct-cost cap (used for many R01 awards) has lost purchasing power since 2001 and what the equivalent cap would need to be in later years when adjusted for BRDPI inflation. Useful for PIs and administrators considering budgeting strategy and policy implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full-modular budget limit ($250,000 direct costs/year)
rubrics_metrics.description: The NIH modular budget system limits requests to $250,000 in direct costs per year for many R01 awards; this 'full-modular' limit has been in place since the system's inception (applications submitted after 6/1/1999) and has not been changed since.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A PI can request more than $250,000 but must use a more detailed budgeting process. The $250,000 full-modular limit is a natural starting point for discussion of the purchasing power of a 'typical' NIH award.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use BRDPI inflation numbers to adjust grant amounts for purchasing power
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust the modular-limit dollar amount year-by-year according to the Biomedical Research and Development Price Index (BRDPI) inflation numbers to measure erosion of purchasing power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRDPI numbers can be downloaded from the NIH Office of Budget. Note that recent BRDPI values (e.g., 2017 and 2018) may be projections; be careful to use the correct projection year when computing equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline year selection for equivalency comparisons (FY2001 for $250k)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a fixed baseline year when saying 'what $250,000 in year X is worth compared to year Y' — the author used FY2001 as the starting point for the $250,000 full-modular amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the baseline year when reporting equivalent dollar amounts; different baselines will change the computed equivalent needed in later years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of purchasing-power erosion (static vs escalated comparisons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two related metrics: red bars showing the reduction in purchasing power of a static $250,000 direct-cost amount over time; black bars showing the amount the full-modular limit would need to be escalated to year-by-year to retain the same purchasing power that $250,000 conferred in the baseline year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present both the absolute loss in purchasing power (what $250k now buys) and the required nominal escalation to restore baseline purchasing power for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimated equivalent FY2018 modular limit (~$413,020)
rubrics_metrics.description: To have the same purchasing power in FY2018 that $250,000 conferred in 2001, the modular limit would need to be increased to approximately $413,020 (the author initially misstated the number, giving a 2021 projection instead).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting equivalent figures, verify which BRDPI projection year was used; the author corrected an earlier error that pulled a 2021 projection instead of the correct FY2018 projection. Report ranges (e.g., $400k–$450k) only with the underlying index clarified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modular cap introduces behavioral and institutional artifacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The modular cap influences applicant and institute behavior, producing artifacts in award sizes and budgeting choices across different NIH institutes and centers (ICs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that the cap can cause clustering of requests at the cap, changes in whether applicants use traditional vs modular budgeting, and IC-specific practices that affect observed award-size growth; consult IC-level analyses (e.g., linked datahound post) for nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shifts in applicant budgeting behavior over time (below-cap → at-cap → traditional budgeting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically many R01 requests were below the modular cap; as purchasing power eroded these disappeared and more requests hit the $250k limit. More recently, some investigators choose traditional budgeting to request >$250k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing award-size trends, consider how applicants' strategic choices (stay below cap, request full modular, or use traditional detailed budgets) change over time in response to purchasing-power erosion.

rubrics_metrics.name: IC practices limiting renewal budget increases (e.g., 'one module' or ~10% rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some institutes/centers apply internal rules that limit how much a competing renewal budget can be raised (reported as 'one module per funding cycle' or roughly 10%), which can prevent investigators who started below the cap from reaching the full-modular level quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for IC-specific policies on allowable budget increases during renewals when projecting investigators' ability to recover purchasing power over successive cycles; these rules are informal/variable and have been reported anecdotally.
